author: Jorge Vela
title: Over 3,600 children detained by ICE, advocates demand action in McAllen - NewsBreak
text:
By Jorge Vela ,
1 hours ago
MCALLEN, Texas ( ValleyCentral ) — Immigration advocates and elected leaders say more than 3,600 children have been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in just the past few months, raising concerns about conditions and access to basic care.
“An injustice continues to happen every day in our community,” said Carlos Garcia Moctezuma, an immigration attorney. “Right now, I have a valid person who has DACA that is detained at a detention center, I have a father who has lived in the United States for 30 years, who has children serving in the United States military, who is detained at a detention center.”
Advocates say many detainees — including children — continue to face daily detention without consistent access to essential resources. The issue drew renewed attention Wednesday as activists gathered in McAllen to call for the release of children currently in custody.
According to Eric Holguin, Texas State Director for UnidosUS, more than 400 children remain in ICE custody, while more than 3,000 others have either been deported or released and in some cases without adequate care, as more than half of those detained in family groups are children.
“These children don’t even have access to basic food and clean water and clean medical care,” Holguin said. “A lot of them are being captured along with their parents detained along with their parents.”
The issue gained widespread attention following the recent detention of a McAllen family. The Gamez-Cuellar parents and their three sons were held in detention centers across South Texas, separated from one another, which is a situation advocates say reflects a broader pattern.
Sylvia Tanguma, president of the McAllen Federation of Teachers, said the children’s father, Luis Antonio Gamez Martinez, described troubling conditions while detained at the Dilley Detention Center.
“Nobody changed their clocks, and the people inside were not aware and so the bulk of them missed breakfast,” Tanguma said. “There was so many little kids crying because they were hungry and they were not being fed and had to wait until lunch time.”
Tanguma said the impact is now extending into classrooms, where fear of detention is contributing to increased student absences.
“That is going to be so hard for them to make up and for the school district to come up with a plan, so they can bring up these kids. That is going to mean a lot after school tutoring for them and more work for the school district because they will have to pay teachers and other personnel to bring these kids back up to par,” Tanguma said.
The issue also extends beyond children.
Earlier this month in Progreso, Carla Gomez said her 74-year-old mother — a legal permanent resident — was detained while crossing the international bridge.
“She was kept there for 10 hours, and after 10 hours, they told me that I could go home, and she was going to be detained by ICE. Initially, they said she was not going to be detained but just checking if everything was good, and I was lied to,” Gomez said.
Gomez said her mother has only a decades-old misdemeanor but now faces detention with limited access to medical care, despite serious health concerns.
“It took two weeks to finally get a medication, but it’s not the one she takes at home, and they are only giving her medication to prevent strokes, which is not the only thing that she needs, and she is not given anything for her kidney infection; she is just given basically Tylenol,” Gomez said.
She is now urging local leaders to take action. Holguin emphasized the need for community involvement.
“It can’t just be, you know, a like or a heart on a social media post. It has to be a tangible action you have to take, like writing to your members of Congress,” he said.
Gomez said her mother remains in federal custody at the El Valle Detention Center. UnidosUS says the public can share their opinions on this issue by clicking here .
